Is JavaScript single-threaded? Then how does it do async work?

The JS engine runs your code on one main thread with one call stack. The host (browser or Node) does async work in the background: network, timers and I/O run on browser threads or, in Node, through libuv (sockets use the OS's non-blocking APIs, timers run in the event loop, and the libuv thread pool handles file I/O, DNS lookups and some crypto). When that work finishes, its callback is queued, and the event loop pushes it onto the stack once the stack is empty: all microtasks first, then one macrotask, then rendering. For real parallel JS, use Web Workers or Node worker_threads, which communicate through message passing or SharedArrayBuffer.
Explain execution context and hoisting at the engine level.

Before running a script or function body, the engine creates an execution context in two phases. In the creation phase it sets up the environment record: var gets undefined, function declarations are stored in full, let, const and class are registered but uninitialized (the TDZ), this is bound, and the outer environment reference is linked. In the execution phase the code runs line by line. "Hoisting" is just the visible effect of the creation phase.
What exactly is a closure? Give a real-world use and a pitfall.

A closure is a function plus a reference to the environment it was defined in. That lets it read and update those variables after the outer function has returned. Use: private state (counters, a bank account, the module pattern), configured callbacks (makeLogger('AUTH')), memoization and debouncing. Pitfall: stale values (a setInterval callback that captured old state), and memory retention, because large objects stay alive as long as the closure does.
How is this determined? What's the priority order?

It depends on the call site. The priority is new > explicit (call, apply, bind) > implicit (obj.method()) > default (undefined in strict mode). Arrow functions skip all of these and take this lexically. A bound function can't be re-bound with call or apply, but new still overrides bind.
prototype vs __proto__ vs Object.create?

Fn.prototype is the object that instances made with new Fn() will inherit from. obj.__proto__ (properly, Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)) is the object's actual internal [[Prototype]] link. Object.create(proto) makes a new object whose [[Prototype]] is proto, without calling a constructor. Object.create(null) gives a "dictionary" object with no inherited keys.
Microtask vs macrotask — can microtasks starve rendering?

Yes. The loop drains the entire microtask queue before it renders or takes the next macrotask. A promise chain that keeps queueing microtasks would freeze the page. Long synchronous work blocks too, so split it into chunks with setTimeout or scheduler.yield(), or move it to a Worker. requestAnimationFrame callbacks run just before the next paint.
What does new do step by step?

- Creates an empty object.
- Sets its [[Prototype]] to Constructor.prototype.
- Calls the constructor with this set to the new object.
- Returns that object, unless the constructor explicitly returns a different object.
ES Modules vs CommonJS?

ESM is static (imports are resolved before the code runs), which enables tree-shaking. It loads asynchronously, has live bindings, is strict by default, and supports top-level await. CJS's require runs synchronously at runtime and copies values. In Node, ESM is used when the file is .mjs or "type":"module". Dynamic import() works in both and returns a promise. Angular and modern bundlers are ESM-first.
How does garbage collection work in JS? How do you find a memory leak?

Mark-and-sweep based on reachability from the roots, with V8 splitting the heap into a young generation (scavenged frequently) and an old generation (mark-compact). Leaks are objects that are unintentionally still reachable: forgotten timers and listeners, detached DOM nodes, global caches, closures. To find one, take heap snapshots before and after an action in DevTools, compare them, and follow the "Retainers" path to see what's holding the object.
Map vs Object; WeakMap vs Map?

Map accepts any key type (objects too), preserves insertion order, has size, is directly iterable, is faster for frequent add and delete, and has no prototype keys that could collide. Object keys are only strings or symbols, and it's what JSON works with. A WeakMap requires object keys and holds them weakly: when the key is garbage-collected, the entry disappears. It isn't iterable. Use it for private data or metadata attached to DOM nodes and objects without causing leaks.
What is the Temporal Dead Zone?

The time between entering a scope and reaching the let, const or class declaration. Accessing the variable during that time throws a ReferenceError. It catches use-before-declare bugs that var's undefined would hide. typeof x also throws inside the TDZ.
Explain event delegation and why it's efficient.

Because events bubble, you can attach one listener to a common ancestor and identify the real source with e.target.closest(selector). Fewer listeners means less memory and faster setup. It also works for elements added later, which is why jQuery's .on('click', '.row', fn) exists. focus and blur don't bubble, so use focusin and focusout.
async vs defer on script tags?

Both download without blocking HTML parsing. async runs as soon as it has downloaded (interrupting the parser), in no guaranteed order, which suits independent scripts like analytics. defer runs after parsing finishes, in document order, before DOMContentLoaded, which suits app scripts that need the DOM. Module scripts are deferred by default.
What is strict mode and what does it change?

Turn it on with "use strict" (it's automatic in modules and classes). It throws on assignment to undeclared variables, sets this to undefined in plain calls, forbids duplicate parameter names and with, throws on writes to read-only properties, and stops eval from leaking variables. You get safer code and more room for engine optimizations.
Why is 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3? How do you handle money?

Numbers are IEEE-754 binary floating point, and 0.1 can't be represented exactly in binary, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with an epsilon (Math.abs(a-b) < Number.EPSILON). For money, store integer minor units (paise) or use a decimal library, and format with Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {style:'currency', currency:'INR'}).
What are Web Workers / Service Workers?

A Web Worker runs JS on a background thread, with no DOM access, and communicates through postMessage. Use it for CPU-heavy work like parsing or image processing. A Service Worker is a programmable network proxy between the page and the network, used for offline caching (PWAs), push notifications and background sync. It requires HTTPS.

Why might setTimeout(fn, 0) run after 50 ms or more?

0 is a minimum, not a promise. The callback must wait for the current task to finish, for every microtask to drain, and for its turn among other tasks. A render may also come first. Nested timers are clamped to 4 ms after five levels, and background tabs are throttled further. To measure time accurately, use performance.now() and do not count ticks.
requestAnimationFrame vs setTimeout for animation?

requestAnimationFrame runs just before the browser paints, is aligned with the display refresh, and pauses in background tabs. A timer is not synchronised with frames, so it can run twice in one frame (wasted work) or miss a frame (jank). Inside rAF, use the timestamp argument to advance the animation by elapsed time, so it runs at the same speed on 60 Hz and 120 Hz screens. Only CSS transform and opacity animations avoid main-thread layout altogether.
What is a long task, and how do you break one up?

A long task is any task over 50 ms. During it the page cannot respond, which hurts INP (Interaction to Next Paint, a Core Web Vital). Options:
- Split the work into chunks and yield between them with await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r)), or await scheduler.yield() where supported.
- Move sustained CPU work into a Web Worker.
- Use requestIdleCallback for low-priority work.
Do not yield using a promise: await Promise.resolve() only queues a microtask, so the browser still cannot render.
Is Node.js single-threaded?

Your JS runs on one thread per isolate, but the process has more. libuv's pool runs file system calls, dns.lookup and some crypto and zlib work (4 threads by default). Network sockets are non-blocking OS calls made from the main thread. V8 also has GC and compiler helper threads. For parallel JS, use worker_threads, or the cluster module to fork multiple processes that share a port.
What are hidden classes and inline caches, and what can you do to help them?

A hidden class describes an object's layout. An inline cache stores, per access site, the offset of a property for the shapes seen so far. Help them by initialising all properties in the constructor in the same order, avoiding delete on hot objects, and passing same-shaped objects through hot functions. Keep arrays to one element type and avoid holes. Treat this as tuning for hot paths, guided by a profiler.
Why does JSON.parse sometimes beat an object literal, and what is lazy parsing?

V8 uses lazy parsing: it pre-parses inner functions only enough to find syntax errors and captured variables, and fully compiles a function on its first call. For large data, JSON's grammar is much simpler than JS, so JSON.parse('...') can be faster than the same data as a JS literal. A practical consequence is that shipping less JS improves start-up more than micro-optimising it.
Scenario: an Angular or React SPA's memory grows on every route change. How do you investigate?

- Reproduce with a repeatable cycle, such as route A to B and back, ten times.
- Compare heap snapshots before and after, and filter for Detached nodes and growing component classes.
- Read the retainer path. The usual holders are subscriptions never unsubscribed, listeners on window or document, intervals, a third-party chart or map that was never destroyed, a singleton service holding an array of components, and caches without limits.
- Fix with the framework's teardown (takeUntilDestroyed, ngOnDestroy) or AbortSignal, then repeat the measurement to confirm.
Memory that grows then falls after a GC is normal. A rising baseline after forced GCs is the sign of a leak.
WeakRef vs WeakMap, and why is relying on GC timing dangerous?

A WeakMap ties a value's life to a key, and you cannot observe when it goes away. A WeakRef lets you test whether an object is still alive, through deref(). GC timing is unspecified and varies across engines and runs, and an object may never be collected before the program ends. So program logic must not depend on it, and a FinalizationRegistry callback is only an extra safety net.
What can't structured clone copy? How is it different from JSON?

It throws DataCloneError on functions and DOM nodes. It keeps Dates, Maps, Sets, RegExps, typed arrays, BigInt, undefined, and circular references, all of which JSON loses or fails on. It drops prototypes (a class instance arrives as a plain object), getters (only the value is copied), and property descriptors. It is defined by the HTML standard, not ECMAScript, and is exposed as structuredClone().
Scenario: a 200 MB CSV must be parsed and displayed in the browser without freezing it. Design it.

- Do not read it all into a string. Use file.stream() and read it in chunks with a TextDecoderStream.
- Parse inside a Web Worker, so the main thread stays responsive.
- Post rows to the page in small batches, using transferable typed arrays where possible, or keep rows in the worker or IndexedDB and send only the requested page.
- Render with a virtual scroller so that only the visible rows exist in the DOM.
- Show progress and support cancelling with worker.terminate().
If only summaries are needed, consider uploading the file and processing it on the server.
Why does SharedArrayBuffer need special headers?

Shared memory lets a thread build a very precise timer, by incrementing a counter in a loop while another thread reads it. That timer makes Spectre-style side-channel attacks practical. Browsers therefore enable SharedArrayBuffer only for cross-origin isolated pages, which guarantees no cross-origin data shares the process. Set Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp, then check self.crossOriginIsolated.
How do you cancel async work in JavaScript?

A promise itself cannot be cancelled, so cancellation is a convention built on AbortController. Pass controller.signal to fetch, addEventListener and your own functions. Your function checks signal.aborted or listens for the abort event, and rejects with signal.reason. signal.throwIfAborted() makes this short. AbortSignal.timeout(ms) aborts by time, and AbortSignal.any([a, b]) combines signals. Remember the distinction in the error name: a manual abort gives AbortError and a timeout gives TimeoutError.
What is a closure's cost compared with a class method?

A closure-based object creates new function objects per instance, while class methods are one function on the prototype. For a million objects that is a real memory difference. Use prototype methods for many instances, and closures for small numbers of objects or for callbacks.
A user still sees the old version of a PWA after a deploy. Why, and how do you fix it?

The browser downloads the new service worker, but it stays in the waiting state while any tab controlled by the old one is open, and the old one keeps serving cached files. Fixes: listen for the new worker (registration.onupdatefound, or Angular's SwUpdate.versionUpdates) and show "A new version is available, reload", then call skipWaiting() and reload. Also make sure sw.js / ngsw.json are served with Cache-Control: no-cache so the update check is not itself cached.
What is the difference between a Service Worker and a Web Worker?

A Web Worker belongs to one page, lives as long as that page, and exists to run heavy computation off the main thread; the page talks to it with postMessage. A Service Worker belongs to an origin and scope, is shared by all tabs, can run when no page is open (push, background sync), and is mainly a network proxy. Neither can access the DOM. The browser can stop an idle service worker at any time, so it must not keep state in global variables; use IndexedDB or the Cache API.
Lighthouse gives 95 but real users complain the page is slow. How can both be true?

Lighthouse is a lab test: one load, one device profile, often with an empty or warm cache, and no logged-in data or slow third-party scripts. Real users have older phones, bad networks, bigger accounts, and they interact, which affects INP and is barely measured by a page-load test. Collect field data with the web-vitals library or a RUM tool, segment by device and page, then reproduce the slow cases in the DevTools Performance panel with CPU throttling.
Why might tree shaking not remove an unused library function?

Common reasons: the library is published as CommonJS; you imported the whole namespace in a way the bundler cannot analyse (import _ from 'lodash' instead of lodash-es named imports); the module has top-level side effects, so the bundler must keep it; or something references it dynamically, for example by string key. Use a bundle analyser (source-map-explorer, esbuild metafile) to see what is actually included.
What causes "Maximum call stack size exceeded"? Does JavaScript have tail call optimisation?

Each function call pushes a frame on the call stack; deep or infinite recursion exceeds the engine's limit (often around ten thousand frames, depending on frame size). ES2015 specified proper tail calls, but only Safari implements them, so you cannot rely on TCO in Chrome or Node. Fixes: convert recursion to a loop with an explicit stack array, use a trampoline, or process in chunks. Another common cause is accidental recursion, such as a setter that assigns to itself or an Angular effect that writes a signal it reads.
preload vs prefetch: what happens if you use them wrongly?

preload is high priority for the current page; preloading things that are not used soon wastes bandwidth and competes with critical resources, and Chrome warns in the console when a preloaded resource is not used within a few seconds. prefetch is idle-time, low priority for a future navigation; using it for something the current page needs makes that resource arrive late. Preloading fonts also needs the crossorigin attribute, or the font is downloaded twice.
